steps.body:
Multiply both sides of P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) by P(B):

P(A ∩ B) = P(B) × P(A | B).

In words: to get **both**, first get B, then get A *in the world where B already happened*. Half the students ride the bus; 40% of those play a sport; so 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20 do both.
A hundred squares, one per percent of the school.

widget.prompt: Shade the students who take the bus **and** play a sport — half the width, then 40% of that strip.
widget.successFeedback: 20 of 100 squares. The rectangle is 0.5 wide and 0.4 tall, and 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20 — the joint probability as an area.
widget.lowFeedback: Smaller than the rectangle. Take half the square (the bus riders), then 40% of that half.
widget.highFeedback: Larger than 0.5 × 0.4. Shading half the square would be P(bus) alone, before the sport condition is applied.

predict.prompt: You'll shade 1/5 of the grid. Will that cover more or less than half of it?
predict.reveal: Half means the numerator is half the denominator — 2.5/5 here — and 1 is less. Probability as shaded area makes the benchmark visible before you count a single cell.

cml.actionGoal: Select regions of an equal-outcome sample space and coordinate area with event probability.

explanationVariants: P(bus and sport) = P(bus) × P(sport | bus) = 0.50 × 0.40 = 0.20. The second factor must be conditional on the first.
Using 0.50 × 0.55 would assume bus riders play sports at the school-wide rate. They do not: their rate is 0.40.

widget.prompt: P(bus) = 0.50, P(sport) = 0.55, P(sport | bus) = 0.40. Which product gives P(bus and sport)?

options.feedback: Right — P(B) × P(A | B). The second factor is measured inside the first event's world.
That multiplies the two marginals, which silently assumes bus riders play sports at the school-wide 55% rate. Their real rate is 40%, so this overstates the joint (0.275 instead of 0.20).
Both of those factors already involve sport, so the product double-counts the sport condition and never uses P(bus).
That is the addition rule, which answers "bus OR sport". For AND you multiply along a condition.

explanationVariants: After a heart leaves, 51 cards remain and only 12 are hearts — the second factor must use the shrunken deck.

widget.prompt: Draw 2 cards without replacing the first. P(both hearts) works out to exactly 1/n. Find **n**.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 13/52 × 13/52 = 1/16 — the with-replacement answer. Without replacement the second draw sees 51 cards, only 12 of them hearts.
That is 1/(13/52) — the first draw alone. The second draw must be conditioned on the first and multiplied in.
That looks like half the deck. Multiply the two draws: (13/52) × (12/51) = 1/17.

steps.body:
The rule works from either end:

P(A ∩ B) = P(B) × P(A | B) = P(A) × P(B | A).

Use whichever conditional you actually know. That freedom is what makes the rule usable — and it is the seed of Bayes' rule, since both products describe the same overlap.

explanationVariants: P(rain and traffic) = P(rain) × P(traffic | rain) = 0.30 × 0.80 = 0.24.
Rain happens 30% of days, and on those days traffic happens 80% of the time. 80% of 30% is 24%.

widget.prompt: P(rain) = 0.30. On rainy days, P(traffic | rain) = 0.80. Find P(rain and traffic).

commonErrors.feedback: That is P(traffic | rain) on its own — the chance of traffic *given* rain. Most days are not rainy, so the joint must be smaller than 0.30.
That is 0.30 + 0.80. Adding would answer "rain OR traffic", and it also exceeds 1 — a sure sign the wrong rule was applied.
That is 0.30/0.80 — dividing instead of multiplying. Division recovers a conditional from a joint; here you already have the conditional.

steps.body: When is multiplying the marginals safe?
explanationVariants: P(A) × P(B) is only the joint when P(B | A) = P(B) — that is, when knowing A tells you nothing about B.
The general rule always needs a conditional as the second factor. Marginal × marginal is a special case, not the default.

widget.prompt: When can you compute P(A and B) as simply P(A) × P(B)?

options.label: When knowing A leaves the chance of B unchanged.
options.feedback: Right — then P(B | A) = P(B), and the general rule collapses to the product of marginals. That condition has a name, coming next chapter.

options.label: Always — that is what "and" means.
options.feedback: The bus students showed otherwise: 0.50 × 0.55 = 0.275, but the true joint is 0.20. Knowing they ride the bus changes their sport rate.

options.label: Whenever A and B cannot both happen.
options.feedback: If they cannot both happen, P(A and B) is 0, and the product of two positive marginals certainly is not 0.

options.label: Whenever A and B have the same probability.
options.feedback: Equal probabilities say nothing about whether one event informs the other. What matters is whether P(B | A) equals P(B).

hints: Draw one ace first: 4 aces in 52 cards.
If that succeeds, the deck now holds 51 cards and only 3 aces.
Multiply the two stages, then write the result as 1/n.
explanationVariants: 12 ordered ace-pairs exist out of 52 × 51 = 2652 ordered draws, and 2652/12 = 221.

widget.prompt: Draw 2 cards without replacement. P(both aces) is exactly 1/n. Find **n**.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 13 × 13, the with-replacement answer (4/52 × 4/52 = 1/169). The first ace is not put back, so the second draw sees 3 aces in 51 cards.
That is 1/(4/52) — only the first draw. The second draw still has to happen, and multiplying by 3/51 makes the event much rarer.
That is 12 × 17, or 52 × 51 divided by 13 — a slip in one of the factors. The clean route: (1/13) × (1/17) = 1/221.

steps.body: AND means multiply — along a condition.
takeaways: P(A ∩ B) = P(B) × P(A | B) = P(A) × P(B | A). Pick the conditional you know.
The second factor lives in the world where the first event already happened — that is why deck sizes shrink.
P(A) × P(B) is a special case that needs justifying, not a default.
steps.teaser: Next: chain the rule down a tree, one draw at a time.

concept.body: Think of it as a two-stage journey. Stage one: how likely is B at all? Stage two: **given you got there**, how likely is A? Multiply the two stages. The second probability must be measured inside the world the first one created.

explanationVariants: Six in ten students own a bike; half of those ride it to school; so three in ten do both.

widget.prompt: 60% of students own a bike. Of the bike owners, 50% ride to school. What fraction of all students own a bike and ride it to school?

commonErrors.feedback: That is the conditional 50% — the rate among bike owners only. Bike owners are just 60% of the school, so the joint must be less than 0.60.
That is 0.60 + 0.50. Adding overshoots (it even exceeds 1); a two-stage AND multiplies.
